Yet the plants are growing.

Welcome to vertical farming—a way of bringing agriculture into the third dimension, and potentially much closer to the people it feeds.

For most of human history, growing more food meant using more land. Vertical farming asks a different question: What if we could grow upward?

That question matters because cities are growing on a planet with limited resources. The United Nations projected in 2018 that roughly 68 percent of the world’s population would live in urban areas by 2050. Meanwhile, agriculture accounts for about 70 percent of global freshwater withdrawals, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization.

Our challenge is not simply to produce more food. It is to produce nutritious food while managing water, land, energy, and a changing climate.

Vertical farming offers one piece of that puzzle.

**What does it actually involve?**

At its simplest, vertical farming means growing crops in stacked layers. The kind we are exploring today combines those layers with a carefully controlled indoor environment.

Think of it as a building where each shelf is a small field—and where farmers can adjust the weather.

LED lights provide the energy plants would normally receive from the sun. Temperature controls keep the air within a suitable range. Ventilation moves air around leaves. Sensors track conditions such as humidity, nutrient levels, and acidity.

Many farms use hydroponics, which means growing plants with their roots supplied by nutrient-rich water rather than soil.

This can sound unnatural until we remember what soil does. Among other things, it anchors roots and holds water and nutrients. Plants still need those resources when soil is removed; farmers simply deliver them another way.

Other farms use aeroponics, where exposed roots receive a nutrient mist.

In both cases, roots also need oxygen. A successful system does more than keep plants wet—it maintains the balance between water, nutrients, and air.

Above the roots, another balance is taking place.

Plants use light to turn water and carbon dioxide into sugars through photosynthesis. LEDs let growers control the timing, intensity, and spectrum of that light. Red and blue wavelengths are particularly useful, although other wavelengths also influence plant growth and development.

The aim is not to leave the lights on as long as possible. It is to provide the right conditions for a particular crop without wasting electricity.

A vertical farmer, then, is part grower, part building operator, and part data interpreter.

**Why bring this into a city?**

Start with water.

On an open field, irrigation water may evaporate, run off, or drain beyond the reach of roots. In a recirculating hydroponic system, water that plants do not take up can be collected and used again. Some indoor farms also recover moisture that plants release into the air.

Well-designed systems can use around 90 percent less water than some conventional growing methods. But that figure needs context: savings depend on the crop, climate, equipment, and what farming system is being used for comparison.

The principle is straightforward. When water stays inside a managed loop, much less needs to be added.

Then there is space.

Imagine ten growing layers occupying the floor area of one field. You have multiplied the growing surface without multiplying the land footprint. Actual productivity also depends on spacing, crop choice, and harvest frequency, but stacking creates a powerful opportunity where land is scarce.

Indoor growing can also continue through winter or periods of extreme outdoor weather. That can make the supply of certain crops more predictable.

And growing closer to consumers can shorten the journey from harvest to plate.

For delicate greens and herbs, that may mean fresher produce, less time in refrigerated transport, and fewer opportunities for spoilage. A city could gain a nearby source of perishable foods while making productive use of suitable existing buildings.

There is a human opportunity here, too. Urban farms can create jobs in cultivation, engineering, maintenance, and distribution. They can give students a place to see biology, nutrition, and technology working together.

Food production becomes something residents can encounter in their own neighborhoods.

**But there is a catch—and it is a substantial one.**

Sunlight arrives at a field without an electricity bill.

Inside a fully enclosed vertical farm, we pay to replace it.

We also pay to remove heat from lights and equipment, control humidity, and move water and air. The same enclosure that gives farmers control creates a major demand for energy.

This is why “grown locally” does not automatically mean “lower carbon.”

A truck journey matters. But so does the electricity used throughout a crop’s life. A nearby indoor lettuce farm powered by a carbon-intensive grid may have a larger climate footprint than a distant outdoor farm, even after transportation is included.

To assess sustainability, we need to look at the whole system.

Where does the power come from? How efficiently is it used? What infrastructure was built? How much produce reaches consumers rather than becoming waste?

More efficient LEDs, better climate controls, and cleaner electricity can improve the answer. They do not make those questions disappear.

Economics presents another constraint. Buildings, equipment, electricity, labor, and maintenance are expensive. Several prominent vertical-farming businesses have entered bankruptcy or restructured in recent years—a reminder that growing a healthy plant and running a healthy business are different achievements.

Crop choice matters enormously.

Leafy greens and herbs are common because they grow relatively quickly, remain compact, and can earn a reasonable price for the space they occupy. Strawberries are another area of development.

Wheat, rice, and maize present a much harder case. These crops supply affordable calories on an enormous scale. Growing them under purchased light is generally difficult to justify economically.

A useful distinction is this: a vertical farm may help supply a city’s salad, but it is unlikely to supply its bread at competitive cost.

That still leaves a meaningful role.

**So where does the transformative potential lie?**

It lies in making our food system more diverse and adaptable.

Cities do not need every meal to come from one type of farm. They can draw on a combination of regional fields, greenhouses, rooftop gardens, and indoor vertical farms. Each has strengths suited to particular crops and places.

In a water-scarce city with access to low-carbon electricity, a recirculating indoor farm may offer significant benefits. Elsewhere, a greenhouse using natural sunlight may make better environmental and financial sense.

Good urban agriculture begins with the needs of a place.

It also begins with the needs of its people. A technologically impressive farm contributes little to food security if its produce is inaccessible to most residents. Affordability, distribution, and community participation deserve as much attention as lights and sensors.

Picture a future city where schools purchase fresh greens from a nearby grower, suitable buildings host productive farms, and urban planners consider food alongside housing, transport, and energy.

That future requires careful choices. It requires measuring results and being honest about costs. But it expands our sense of what a city can do.

We usually imagine cities as places that consume what the countryside produces. Vertical farming invites us to imagine cities participating more directly in growing their food.

Its greatest promise is not that every skyscraper becomes a farm. It is that we gain another useful way to nourish urban life while easing particular pressures on land and water.

The question is no longer simply, “Can we grow food upward?”

We can.

The more important question is, “Where does growing upward help us build a better city?”

Thank you."}
